headline: New Hampshire heating-aid agencies brace for surge as oil nears $6 a gallon
dek: Agencies report more first-time applicants in several counties as heating oil approaches $6 a gallon and state assistance will not be released until December 1.
body: New Hampshire agencies that distribute heating assistance are preparing for a rush of first-time applicants as heating oil approaches $6 per gallon. [New Hampshire Public Radio](https://www.nhpr.org/business/2026-10-12/high-fuel-costs-nh-newhampshire-heating-assistance) reported Monday that Southwestern Community Services has seen about 200 more applications from new households in Cheshire and Sullivan counties than at the same point last year. The agency's director of energy services said more working families are applying and qualifying. Community Action Partnership serving Hillsborough and Rockingham counties is also seeing new applicants and expects a larger surge, NHPR reported.

Those agency observations are not a statewide tally, but they offer an early view of how the price shock is reaching households that have not previously used fuel assistance. The applicants include people who are employed but have less room in their budgets after food, housing, transportation and utility costs. Providers told NHPR that some residents are worried about making it through the full heating season, not just paying for a single delivery.

The underlying price data are stark. The [U.S. Energy Information Administration's Oct. 7 release](https://www.eia.gov/petroleum/heatingoilpropane/) lists New Hampshire residential heating oil at $5.976 per gallon for the week of Oct. 5, excluding taxes. That was $2.438 higher than a year earlier, a year-over-year increase of about 69%. NHPR described the current price as nearly $6 per gallon and about $2.50 above last year's level. A household's actual delivered price can differ by supplier, contract, delivery charge and location, so the EIA average is a statewide reference point rather than an individual bill.

The [EIA's October Winter Fuels Outlook](https://www.eia.gov/pressroom/releases/press593.php) also forecasts that households that primarily heat with oil will spend about 21% more on the fuel this winter than last winter. The agency expects heating-oil prices to average more than 30% higher, with a milder Northeast winter partly offsetting the added cost. Those are national and regional forecasts, not a prediction of how much any particular New Hampshire family will spend, but they help explain why community-action agencies are seeing pressure before sustained cold arrives.

New Hampshire's Fuel Assistance Program is the state's version of the federally funded Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program. NHPR reported that households with income up to roughly 60% of the state's median income may qualify—about $49,000 for a one-person household and nearly $94,000 for a family of four. The maximum benefit for the season has increased to $2,500, up $323 from the prior maximum, according to figures cited by NHPR from the [New Hampshire Bulletin](https://www.newsfromthestates.com/article/oil-prices-soar-more-nh-residents-fall-behind-their-heating-bills). Southwestern Community Services told NHPR its average benefit is about $1,200, which means many awards will be below the program maximum.

The [Community Action Partnership Hillsborough and Rockingham](https://www.caphr.org/services/fuel-assistance) program page describes the assistance as a grant of $188 to $2,500 for eligible homeowners and renters. Qualifying deliveries can include oil, kerosene, propane, wood or coal, and the benefit is generally paid to the fuel vendor or, in some cases, the landlord. It is not unrestricted cash, and the program is designed to supplement heating costs rather than cover every bill. Residents should confirm current income rules and local application procedures with the community-action agency serving their county.

Timing is becoming part of the problem. NHPR reported that benefits will not be released until Dec. 1, and agencies are urging eligible households to apply as soon as possible so applications can be processed before that date. Terra Rogers of Southwestern Community Services told NHPR that people who are already out of oil or running low will still have to wait for the state program; residents with an immediate emergency should contact their town or city welfare office for help.

The next pressure point is whether the aid pool can keep up with demand. Higher benefits do not guarantee that every household will receive the maximum, and an award that helps with one delivery may not cover repeated fills during a long or expensive winter. Federal lawmakers could change funding or eligibility, but no such change is enacted in the reporting reviewed for this update. For now, New Hampshire households facing a narrow budget and high fuel costs have the clearest practical step available: apply early, use the agency's eligibility determination, and seek local emergency assistance before a tank or account reaches a crisis.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: NH heating aid agencies brace for more applicants
seoDescription: New Hampshire agencies report more first-time heating-aid applicants as EIA puts Oct. 5 oil at $5.976 per gallon and benefits wait until Dec. 1.
